cim: Your AI agent prompt shouldn’t read like an essay
cim_eredeti: Your AI agent prompt shouldn’t read like an essay
szoveg_eredeti:

Even the best frontier AI models aren’t very good at following a long essay of instructions. David Cox, Vice President for AI Models at IBM Research, joins the We Love Open Source podcast to share why agent building is shifting from prompting back to programming, what his dad’s punch cards have to do with the future of developers, and what’s holding enterprises back from deploying AI.

If you’ve ever built an AI agent, you’ve probably written one of those long, essay-style prompts full of do this, don’t do that, and be sure to handle this case. David sees two problems with that approach, and only one of them is about maintainability. He shares the shift he’s seeing in how developers break those prompts apart, what traditional computing still does better than any LLM, and what the finished program ends up looking like.

David doesn’t think AI will replace developers, and his reasoning starts with his dad and a stack of punch cards. He uses that story to explain where he thinks developer work is headed, and why he’s careful not to guess too far ahead. It’s also the moment that gets the biggest laugh of the interview, thanks to one very slow way to get an answer from AI.

David calls this a best of times, worst of times moment for enterprises trying to put AI to work. The technology is moving fast, but that’s only half of the story. He breaks down what makes deployment so hard right now, from security to mistakes that would be embarrassing or expensive, and why he thinks we’re still in the early stages. He also shares the kind of “better models” he thinks enterprises need right now, and they’re not the AI kind.

David also shares what has to change about the hardware and power behind AI, and how a folding phone keeps him productive when his travel schedule starts to resemble the president’s plane at DEFCON 4. Watch the full episode to hear why he says he’s not really a tools guy, and his Mac-and-Android picks in the Hot Fix Minute.
